claims.text: In a straight-line history, `git log -- <path>` shows every commit that changed that path (in general, the commits that explain how it came to be); the `--` marks what follows as paths, which matters when a name could also be read as a branch.
claims.source_hint: git-log documentation, SYNOPSIS and '[--] <path>...'; gitcli documentation on disambiguating paths from revisions

claims.text: `git log --oneline` prints one line per commit, abbreviated id then subject, in reverse chronological order by default.
claims.source_hint: git-log documentation, --oneline and Commit Ordering (reverse chronological default)

claims.text: `git blame <file>` annotates each line of the file with the commit that last modified that line, that commit's author and author date, and the line number before the line content.
claims.source_hint: git-blame documentation, DESCRIPTION and THE DEFAULT FORMAT

claims.text: Blame attributes a line to the last commit that changed its content, so a re-indentation or a reformatting becomes the answer for every line it touched even when behaviour did not change (whole-file renames are followed automatically; moved or copied blocks need -M/-C).
claims.source_hint: git-blame documentation, DESCRIPTION ('followed across whole-file renames') and -w/-M/-C options

claims.text: `git reset [<mode>] <commit>` moves the current branch to <commit>; `--soft` leaves index and working tree, `--mixed` (the default) also resets the index, `--hard` also resets the working tree, discarding changes to tracked files; untracked files stay unless they are in the way of a tracked file.
claims.source_hint: git-reset documentation, DESCRIPTION and the --soft/--mixed/--hard table

claims.text: `git revert <commit>` records a new commit that reverses the changes introduced by <commit>; the reverted commit stays in the history, and the branch gains a commit rather than losing one.
claims.source_hint: git-revert documentation, DESCRIPTION ('record some new commits to reverse the effect')

claims.text: `git revert --no-edit` uses the commit message Git composes instead of opening an editor; `git switch --quiet -c <name> <start-point>` creates a branch at <start-point> and stands on it.
claims.source_hint: git-revert documentation, --no-edit; git-switch documentation, -c/--create, <start-point> and --quiet

claims.text: `HEAD` names the commit checked out. The reflog records recent updates of HEAD and each branch tip locally (entries expire after 30 or 90 days by default); `<name>@{n}` is where that name stood n moves ago; switching branches adds entries to HEAD's log, not the branch's.
claims.source_hint: git-reflog documentation, DESCRIPTION and 'show' subcommand; gitrevisions documentation, <refname>@{<n>}

claims.text: Reflogs record updates of HEAD and of branch tips in the local repository, so a commit found through the reflog is recovered from this repository alone, without asking the server.
claims.source_hint: git-reflog documentation, DESCRIPTION ('in the local repository')

claims.text: A commit that no name reaches is not removed at once: gc keeps what reflog entries name, and those expire after 30 or 90 days by default, so a commit a reset moved away from stays for weeks to months and the reflog can still name it.
claims.source_hint: git-gc documentation, DESCRIPTION and gc.pruneExpire / gc.reflogExpire

claims.text: `git commit --amend` replaces the tip commit with a new commit carrying the corrected message or content; the new commit has a different id, and the old commit is no longer reachable from the branch tip although the reflog still names it.
claims.source_hint: git-commit documentation, --amend ('replace the tip of the current branch by creating a new commit')

claims.text: `HEAD~2` names the commit two generations back along first parents from HEAD; a merge commit's first parent is the commit the branch stood on when the merge was made.
claims.source_hint: gitrevisions documentation, <rev>~<n>; git-merge documentation (merge commit parents, current branch first)

claims.text: In `git log`, `--grep` keeps commits whose message matches, `-1` limits output to one commit; `%h` abbreviated id, `%H` full id, `%ad` author date, `%s` subject, `%n` newline; `--date=short` prints YYYY-MM-DD. In the shell, `$( … )` inserts a command's output and `>/dev/null` discards output.
claims.source_hint: git-log documentation, --grep, -<number>, --date=short and PRETTY FORMATS (%h, %ad, %s, %H, %n)

claims.text: `git blame` and `git log --oneline` abbreviate object ids to different lengths, so the same commit reads as b3472f64 in the blame output and b3472f6 in the log output of the same run.
claims.source_hint: outputs/stage-0/scripts/git/blame-and-log.txt at stage-0, the log block and the last blame line; git-blame documentation, --abbrev

claims.text: `git push` sends a branch's new commits to the shared repository; other copies get them only when they next fetch from it. After moving a branch name backwards with reset, the next push of that branch is rejected as non-fast-forward unless forced.
claims.source_hint: git-push documentation, 'Note about fast-forwards' and --force; git-fetch documentation, DESCRIPTION

claims.text: Opinion: when the commit is already on the server, revert is the shape to choose, because it only adds a commit, while reset asks every other copy of the repository to forget commits it already has.
claims.source_hint: outline item 2 of foundation.l2.git-history-and-recovery; git-revert documentation, DESCRIPTION (contrast with git reset)

claims.text: Opinion: amending and squashing belong before a commit is shared; once others hold it, add a commit instead of replacing one.
claims.source_hint: outline item 4 of foundation.l2.git-history-and-recovery; git-rebase documentation, RECOVERING FROM UPSTREAM REBASE

claims.text: A commit's id is computed from its content, so replacing a commit's message or parent yields a different commit; this lesson reuses that fact from foundation.l2.git-mental-model for amend and squash.
claims.source_hint: gitglossary, entries 'commit' and 'object name'; foundation.l2.git-mental-model summary line on ids

claims.text: Squashing replaces several commits with one commit carrying their combined change, so the result is a new commit with a new id; a rebase likewise moves the branch name onto new commits, which is why the reflog entry from before it is the way back.
claims.source_hint: git-rebase documentation, INTERACTIVE MODE ('squash' command) and RECOVERING FROM UPSTREAM REBASE; git-reflog documentation, DESCRIPTION
